title: How fast do excavators, skid steers and dozers lose value, and which machine size costs most per tonne?
lede: heavy-equipment market, milestone 1a, real auction data: on 363,718 US auction sales (1989-2012) a two-way fixed-effects model puts annual depreciation at 6.5% for track excavators against 3.8 to 5.0% for skid steers, wheel loaders, dozers, graders and backhoes; among nearly new excavators price rises only with weight to the power 0.63, so a 1 t mini excavator sells for about 11,000 dollars a tonne against about 2,000 at 45 t
summary: Track 25's first market step, on real data: where the money goes in owning a heavy machine. The Kaggle Blue Book for Bulldozers file (412,698 US auction sales, 1989 to 2012; 363,718 kept with a valid year made) is fitted per machine class with log price on age plus model and sale-year fixed effects, so depreciation is measured within a model and within a year (inflation and the market cycle swept out), with 95% intervals clustered by model. Annual depreciation: track excavators 6.5% [6.2, 6.8], backhoe loaders 5.0%, dozers 4.6%, motor graders 4.5%, wheel loaders 4.2%, skid steers 3.8% [3.4, 4.3]. Every class loses value two to three times faster in its first ten years (6.0 to 8.8% a year) than after (1.6 to 3.8%). Among track excavators 0 to 3 years old sold 2009 to 2012, sale price rises with operating weight to the power 0.634 [0.604, 0.665] (2,805 sales, 395 models), so price per tonne falls with size: about 11,000 dollars a tonne under 2 t, 5,400 at 3 to 4 t and 1,900 at 40 to 50 t. That is the market side of the open-machine question: per tonne, compact machines carry the most price above their steel. Prices are nominal auction prices, not new list prices or dealer margins; the data ends in 2012; Kaggle's competition terms could not be opened from the session, so only aggregate statistics are published and the raw file is not redistributed. Research, not a valuation or advice.
